articles.title_orig: Ambassador Xie Feng delivered video remarks at the seventh U.S.-China Hong Kong Forum
articles.title_zh: Ambassador Xie Feng delivered video remarks at the seventh U.S.-China Hong Kong Forum
articles.source: 中华人民共和国驻美利坚合众国大使馆
articles.content_orig:
On November 16, 2026, Chinese Ambassador to the United States Xie Feng delivered video remarks at the seventh U.S.-China Hong Kong Forum.
Ambassador Xie noted this has been a landmark year for China-U.S. relations. President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump exchanged state visits within six months, a historic first, opening new opportunities for the bilateral relationship.
Ambassador Xie shared three thoughts in light of the forumâs theme, "Tomorrow Will Be Better Than Today". First, follow the strategic guidance of the two Presidents and chart a steady course toward a brighter future for China-U.S. relations. In Beijing, the two Presidents agreed on a new vision of building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability. In Washington, they gave that vision greater substance through the principles of "respect, fairness and reciprocity", offering clearer strategic guidance for how our two countries should get along. Both sides should make concerted efforts and turn the vision into reality. Second, strengthen mutually beneficial cooperation to build a future of shared prosperity. China and the United States have deeply intertwined interests. Helping each other succeed through win-win cooperation is the only right choice. It is hoped that Hong Kong will make full use of its unique strengths, deepen its engagement in China-U.S. cooperation, explore new opportunities, and become a leading hub for win-win partnerships. Third, build more bridges between the two peoples for a brighter future. Ambassador Xie encouraged the China-United States Exchange Foundation and friends from all walks of life to continue to bring the two peoples closer through two-way exchanges, fostering the goodwill and fresh momentum that will sustain China-U.S. relations in the years ahead.
The forum was co-hosted by the China-United States Exchange Foundation and the Chinese People's Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries in Hong Kong. More than 300 delegates attended the forum, including former dignitaries, along with representatives from the strategic and business communities as well as think tanks from China, the United States and other countries.

articles.title_orig: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
articles.title_zh: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.
The federal government is stepping up scrutiny of semiconductor exports to ensure that such shipments don't bypass existing regulations prohibiting their sale to certain U.S. competitors, such as China. The temporary regulations follow last week's shock resignation of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a subordinate at the company.
Huang's exit has heightened concerns that China and other nations could access Nvidia's advanced chips by renting computing resources through data centers in Southeast Asia.
"The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday. "The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security."
In addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, the new rule will require licenses for exporting, re-exporting, or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. BIS said such nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."
The interim rule notes that advances in cloud computing have made it easier for foreign nations to access American AI computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers in countries not subject to U.S. export restrictions.
The Commerce Department wants to "ensure that computing power, based on U.S. technology located in foreign data centers, is not used in a manner contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests," the rule states.
The rule aims to align remote-access protections with existing controls governing physical access to sensitive American technology, the Commerce Department said.
Existing regulations on chip exports apply only to the most advanced semiconductors. "Selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing," President Trump said in remarks at the White House on Monday.
Mr. Trump is heading to Asia on Monday, where he's expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Chinese officials have said the country was not involved in Huang's affair with the suspected spy.

articles.title_orig: Stocks Fall Before Nvidia Earnings, Anthropic IPO: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks Fall Before Nvidia Earnings, Anthropic IPO: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
The market is unable to divert its attention from anything not related to the ongoing saga that is Nvidia and its embattled former CEO Jensen Huang. It's understandable, given both the detail of the story and Nvidia impact on the market. It remains the tech story du jour, and it's getting plenty of ink.
I think investors should remember there are other big names reporting this week outside of Nvidia that deserve time and attention. One such name is The Walt Disney Company (DIS) .
After a prolonged period of strategic transitions, the company may finally be turning the corner. Driven by a renewed focus on the bottom line, management's cost discipline now supports a runway for double-digit earnings-per-share (EPS) gains through fiscal 2027, even as it continues to trade at about its 5-year average forward multiple of 14.3x, well below the broad market multiple of more than 18x. Trading back to a market multiple, justified if it establishes above-market EPS growth, suggests ~26% upside, which is also consistent with a sum-of-the-parts analysis that points to an intrinsic valuation of $140 to $160 per share versus the Friday, November 13th closing price of $118.97.
Disney reports Tuesday before the bell.
Despite broader macroeconomic anxieties, the theme park and cruise divisions are showing surprisingly resilient demand. Domestically, the metrics are highly encouraging: attendance is climbing, and more importantly, per-capita spending continues to rise.
On the digital front, Direct-to-Consumer (DTC) Disney's streaming margins currently sit in the low teens, respectable given the segment's previous lack of profits. But the real upside scenario requires looking ahead: if Disney can scale these DTC margins to 20% or higher, the stock could at least trade at a multiple comparable to streaming king Netflix (which would imply a share price of ~ $139 or so.
Part of the reason the studio segment remains a mixed bag is that, while there are periodic blockbuster bright spots, Disney's theatrical recovery remains uneven overall. Furthermore, legacy media continues its secular decline. The pay-TV industry has likely lost around 40 million subscribers—representing a staggering 40% erosion of the user base since 2015—and will likely lose more this year. However, the critical takeaway for investors is that the pace of cord-cutting is finally slowing down.
With linear TV stabilizing, the parks firing on all cylinders, and streaming marching toward higher profitability, Disney offers a highly asymmetric risk-reward profile. The magic is returning to Disney's financials, and the current share price heavily discounts a business fundamentally engineered for double-digit growth.
Right now, the options market is pricing a ~6% move by the end of the week (the company reports Tuesday, pre-open), which is below the 8 quarter median move of 7.4%. Anticipating a "vol crush" after earnings, I like selling December premium to help finance the purchase of a longer-dated call - a diagonal call/spread risk reversal.
When selecting an option trade consider the key things that affect its value and how those things differ from simply buying (or selling) the underlying asset. For these option trades, let's consider three sensitivities (Greeks): Delta, the rate at which the option position changes in value for changes in the underlying price. Theta, or decay, which measures how much the value of an option declines as time passes, and Vega, the change in an option's price associated with changes in the implied volatility of an option.
In the case of the diagonal risk reversal each of these factors plays into the structure to our benefit. The delta of the structure is less than 100, meaning that the p&l associated with moves up or down will be less for one spread than they would be for 100 shares of stock.
We like this because the stock has already had a decent run recently, and the option structure will lose less than the stock will if it gives that back. Because nearer dated expiration decay more rapidly as a percentage of the options value than longer dated options do (and out of the money options also exhibit accelerated decay), the shorter dated December options we're selling should decay in value more quickly than the longer dated March options we are buying, even though the March option has a higher premium. Vega can work in our favor as well due to "vol crush". When option premiums are elevated due to a catalyst such as earnings we should expect that much of that premium will be sucked out or crushed once the event has passed.
This will impact both the December and March options to a degree, but remember that the March options also capture another earnings event in February, so some measure of event variance (elevated option premium) will remain in the March expiration to account for that.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Falls Again. It Doesn’t Need a Jensen Huang Comeback to Thrive.
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Falls Again. It Doesn’t Need a Jensen Huang Comeback to Thrive.
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.
The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss internal matters. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.
Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia.
Over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed coming back with allies. Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that Huang had not discussed a comeback with him.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on speculation on Sunday.
Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO.
An online petition calling for his reinstatement has drawn 180,000 signatures as well as support from major figures including Elon Musk , Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.
President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Jensen Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia.
"It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns.
On Friday, a representative for Nvidia's board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi, Putin to discuss ’world peace’, China says
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi, Putin to discuss ’world peace’, China says
articles.content_orig:
Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda, but Trump says denuclearisation, Iran war, trade and Ukraine will be among topics
The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.
The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global powerbroker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he would be speaking to his Chinese and Russian counterparts about denuclearisation, the war in Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. US officials had earlier indicated that Trump would not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the trip.
Many, including the UN secretary general, António Guterres, had hoped the trilateral talks would be used to discuss reductions in nuclear arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.
In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.
China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items.
“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said its foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”
The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.”
Guterres said that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”. However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough.
Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”.
The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian.
after newsletter promotion
China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”.
Trump’s remarks that he wanted to discuss Ukraine could stoke fears voiced by the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that the trilateral talks could turn into a “Yalta 2, 3, 4 with a redistribution of influence”. Zelenskyy was referring to the 1945 pact between the US, UK and Soviet Union that created spheres of influence in Europe after the second world war.
“Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” Trump said. He also deflected criticism of Putin in his remarks, saying the Kremlin leader could be “a lot tougher” in Ukraine and that he was already “backing down”.
US officials had said Trump was not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.
For Xi, much of the political benefit will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC .
The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion.
Sari Arho Havrén, of the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X : “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

articles.title_orig: The delicate balance in America’s AI chip war with China
articles.title_zh: The delicate balance in America’s AI chip war with China
articles.content_orig:
Americans are anxious about artificial intelligence . In the midterm elections , they voted to slow down its expansion. Forty local ballot measures in 10 states promise to tighten restrictions on data-center construction, with overwhelming public support. Measures to limit development of data centers won more than 70% of the vote in 30 of these electoral contests. A 2026 survey by Pew Research Center found that about 52% of Americans were more concerned than excited about the growing use of AI in daily life, up from 37% in 2021. Only 9% were more excited than concerned, and roughly six in ten said they wanted more control over how AI is used in their lives.
The sources of anxiety about AI are many: the safety of increasingly powerful systems and the ability to control them; the fear of job displacement; surveillance and the loss of privacy; a rising tide of misinformation and deep fakes; the enormous amounts of electricity and water that the data centers consume; and the concentration of wealth and power in a handful of companies that own the frontier AI models.
Until now, anxiety about the role of AI in geopolitical competition has largely been confined to policy circles. But the possibility that Jensen Huang, who resigned as chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday, may have been compromised in a potential espionage scandal has brought that anxiety into the broader public sphere, fueling a frenzy over AI and the competition between the United States and China.
China is at the center of arguably two of the world’s most consequential economic and political developments: its dominance in global trade and its formidable AI capabilities. China and America are AI superpowers, but their strengths differ. America leads in computing power, thanks largely to Nvidia’s advanced chips. China is catching up fast in AI models. The economic and geopolitical implications of this competition are enormous.
There is another dimension to this competition: the economic effects of China’s trade dominance and the rising role of AI in the economy could reinforce each other and produce greater impact than either would have alone. China’s trade dominance is well-known. Two decades earlier, the economists David H. Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon H. Hanson gave that anxiety a name when they coined the term “ China Shock ” to describe the impact of the massive increase in Chinese exports to the U.S. in the early 2000s. The surge contributed to a sharp decline in American manufacturing and the loss of more than two million jobs in certain regions of the United States. Over the past two decades, the so-called China Shock has gone global, as Chinese exports have surged around the world without a comparable rise in China’s imports.
The world may soon experience the convergence of two enormous economic shocks, each reinforcing the other in terms of their direction and magnitude: The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock. The consequences of AI-driven productivity growth remain contested. But the fear is that AI will enable companies to dramatically increase output without employing more people or raising the income of ordinary citizens. The China Shock has a similar effect. China has become a dominant force in advanced manufacturing in electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels, artificial intelligence, and robotic technology. But China’s growing competitiveness has led to a global surge of Chinese exports without a corresponding global surge of Chinese imports.
On top of the China Shock, the AI Productivity Shock could further widen the gap between global supply and demand, and create new economic imbalances and strains on a scale the world has not witnessed.
The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock share one critical feature: both can produce a glut of output without generating a corresponding increase in demand. In China, production has grown faster than consumption; with AI, the fear is that the technology will generate wealth without creating jobs. In both cases, the gains tend to flow to the owners of capital—and in China’s case, also to the government—rather than to workers and households.
But the iron law of economics still holds: supply requires demand, and an economy can absorb a large increase in output only if enough people have the income to buy what it produces. Economists have long described it as a problem of effective demand: the recognition that supply does not automatically create its own demand. For that to happen, greater production and supply have to translate into more jobs and higher incomes.
Whether AI will create such an imbalance is still a matter of debate. Optimists point to earlier waves of automation. Technologies such as the tractor and the spreadsheet displaced certain kinds of work but eventually helped create other kinds of work and generated jobs and additional income for workers. Only time will tell whether AI, which differs significantly from earlier technologies, will follow that pattern. What we do know is that this optimistic scenario of technological progress has yet to deliver the gains in employment and household purchasing power in China.
China is now regarded as one of the world’s leading technological powers. In some industries, China’s factories are producing more than the global demand put together. China makes more than 80% of the world’s solar panels, and its factories can turn out roughly twice as many modules in a year as the entire planet installs. In batteries, China’s manufacturing capacity is already more than double the current global demand. One projection suggests that, by 2030, China alone could produce more batteries than the whole world will use.
But China’s technological advancement is far more visible in what its factories can produce than in what its households can afford to buy and consume. Youth unemployment in the country is rising, and domestic consumption has stagnated. The unemployment rate among urban Chinese aged 16 to 24 climbed to a record 18.9 % in August 2025, according to official statistics. The real figure is likely to be much higher.
Economic progress is defined by progress in both production and consumption. These two areas of human activity move in tandem with each other and are mutually reinforcing. Faster productivity leads to rising output , which raises incomes and allows households to buy more of what is being produced. Historically, before the age of AI, this has been the case. The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock may break that connection. What made, and continues to make, the China Shock so disruptive is the immense disparity between the scale of China’s exports and its purchases from the rest of the world. China’s imports consist largely of agricultural products, minerals, and energy products that it cannot produce in sufficient quantities on its soil.
China’s exports lower prices for consumers abroad, a benefit on the expenditure side. But households need income to consume, and that income comes from the production side of the economy. But the Chinese economy is not generating a corresponding increase in income for the rest of the world by importing more from them and boosting their production. China has roughly 35% of the world’s manufacturing capacity but accounts for about just 11% of global consumption. Household consumption in the country amounts to a mere 39% of its GDP, compared with 68% in America. This imbalance is unsustainable—for both China and the world.
Low domestic consumption forces Chinese businesses to sell more abroad, often at cutthroat prices. Cheaper imports benefit consumers abroad, but when local companies close or cut jobs,

articles.title_orig: Warsh Says Fed Is Gaming Out How AI Could Reshape Economy
articles.title_zh: Warsh Says Fed Is Gaming Out How AI Could Reshape Economy
articles.content_orig:
[The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.
Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road."
"I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.
In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.
Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.
In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.
At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint."
"After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."
The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.
Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.
Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.
The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

articles.title_orig: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
articles.title_zh: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year
US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.
Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.
It created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI rollout, but the BBC has been told Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang.
Meanwhile the Trump administration on Monday said it will further restrict China's âaccess to AI chips from companies like Nvidia.
Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".
The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models.
The move came ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jingping.
The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted to China.
The president's comments on Huang came after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.
However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , external , though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A person familiar with the thinking of Nvidia's board told the BBC its directors are not interested in bringing Huang back to lead the company.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.
"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X. , external
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Moves to Close A.I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Moves to Close A.I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Trump heads to Asia for trade, nuclear talks with China and Russia
articles.title_zh: Trump heads to Asia for trade, nuclear talks with China and Russia
articles.content_orig:
Washington — President Trump is setting off Monday for a multi-day swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.
Ahead of his departure, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.
The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first between the three leaders , is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.
Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.
The president will first head to the Philippines, where the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit is being held. Mr. Trump will meet with Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.
On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.
Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.
"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.
As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking. Mr. Trump is not expected to speak about the 4 ½-year war in Ukraine during the summit.
Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang , the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.
Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.
"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.
When asked Monday if Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.
Both Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are traveling with the president. Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.
Seiji  Yamashita contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: 'A beautiful woman': Trump unsure Nvidia CEO had affair with Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: 'A beautiful woman': Trump unsure Nvidia CEO had affair with Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:

President Donald Trump said Monday that he would welcome the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia - days after the chipmaker's co-founder was forced out over an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman - and insisted that no one had proven the woman was a spy.
"There's a big group of people that would like him to return," Trump told reporters as he left the White House to travel to Asia ahead of his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin later this week.
“I think having Jensen go back, a lot of people are asking Jensen. They think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea. I recommended Tim Cook, who, as you know, built Apple, I recommended Tim Cook to go and do a job,” Trump continued.
Huang resigned last week after acknowledging an affair with Alice Huang — no relation — a businesswoman that U.S. officials have described as a suspected asset of China's Ministry of State Security.
The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined she had been recruited by the spy agency and tasked with influencing Huang to push Nvidia toward selling Beijing more of its advanced chips. The Times also reported Jensen Huang’s second affair, with a Nvidia subordinate, moved the company’s board to force him out last week.
In the days since, allies of the former Nvidia boss have been attempting to rally support for his return with an online petition that has thus far garnered more than 100,000 signatures, including from Nvidia shareholders and employees.
Tesla and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the founder and chief executive of the video game publisher Epic Games , were among major industry figures supporting an open letter calling for his return.
But Nvidia sources told CNBC on Monday that the company’s board is not considering bringing him back and is instead focused on a probe into whether his actions harmed American national security.
Pressed repeatedly on whether he accepted the U.S. intelligence on Alice Huang, Trump questioned it.
"I don't know that she's a spy at all. Nobody's proven that," he said. "He probably shouldn't have been doing, on a personal basis, what he did. You know, from — who knows? That's a different story. But nobody's proven that she's a spy. She may not be a spy."
Trump earlier offered a broader version of the same claim. "Usually what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Trump said. "I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
Asked whether he trusted the U.S. intelligence that the woman was a Chinese agent, and whether Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him so, Trump said he had not heard it.
"Who told me that? ... I haven't heard that. I haven't heard that," he said. "No, I don't know that she is a spy."
The president’s claims do not square exactly with what is publicly known about U.S. officials’ concerns over the affair.
According to The New York Times, Rubio was so alarmed by what intelligence officials were learning about Alice Huang through electronic surveillance that he drafted a classified memorandum on her alleged recruitment and briefed Trump on it aboard Air Force One in May, en route to China.
But Trump brushed aside warnings from Rubio and nonetheless pressed ahead with a relationship that saw Huang become a frequent White House visitor after donating $25 million to the president's ballroom project.
The president defended the decision to keep selling chips to China and brushed aside the suggestion that his closeness to Huang had endangered national security. "It was not put at risk," he said Monday, before pivoting to a claim that the country "is now stronger than ever before."
Trump also dismissed statements from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC last week that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick resisted putting Megaspeed - a China-linked company run by Alice Huang and thought to be a pass-through to help Beijing evade export controls - on his department’s “Entity List” of firms not allowed to purchase American products.
Asked about that, Trump said Lutnick "might have delayed it, but he was doing that because ... you could have a blowup with China."
"One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China. Different views," Trump said, declining to say whether he would replace Lutnick, who is traveling with him to China aboard Air Force One despite the scandal surrounding him and is scheduled to testify on the Nvidia affair before Congress in the next few weeks.
Huang was barred from selling Nvidia's most advanced processors, including its Blackwell line, to China, a restriction Trump defended while playing down its stakes.
"The only thing he was able to sell to China were chips that were sort of obsolete, a little bit like our avionics," Trump said. "Selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing."
The president said he might raise the alleged spying operation with Chinese President Xi Jinping when the two leaders meet on Thursday but would not commit to doing so when pressed by reporters.
"I'll ask him what I want to ask him," he said.

articles.title_orig: 'No money left': French far-right leader Le Pen vows to cut off Ukraine aid if elected president
articles.title_zh: 'No money left': French far-right leader Le Pen vows to cut off Ukraine aid if elected president
articles.content_orig:
European leaders need urgently to prepare for a far-right French president who would cut off Kyiv’s financial lifeline
E urope is consumed by two debates that matter less than it thinks, while neglecting one that matters enormously. The first is who should represent the EU in negotiations with Russia. This is largely irrelevant because there is little prospect of serious Ukraine peace talks before the end of winter - despite the fanfare that has surrounded discussions in Abu Dhabi this week. Russia has powerful incentives to escalate the war over the coming months in an attempt to break Ukraine’s economy and civilian morale.
The second is Donald Trump’s approach to Ukraine. This matters less than it once did – and not only because he is now more constrained by a Democratic Congress. Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump has provided no new US military aid to Kyiv. American weapons sales remain important to Ukraine’s war effort, but Trump’s military interventions in the Middle East have further strained supplies of the weapons Ukraine needs most – notably Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine does remain heavily dependent on US early warning intelligence , particularly to detect incoming Russian ballistic missiles, a capability Europe is unlikely to replicate fully before 2030. But the broader point stands: the US is a less indispensable partner to Ukraine than it was two years ago.
The debate European leaders are neglecting is much closer to home: what happens if Marine Le Pen wins France’s presidential election in six month’s time?
A president Le Pen would suspend France’s bilateral aid to Ukraine. More consequentially, her opposition to increasing France’s contribution to the EU budget could jeopardise EU-wide funding. Le Pen is threatening to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget, including a proposed €100bn facility for Ukraine. This is the mechanism through which the EU hopes to sustain Kyiv financially beyond 2028.
A Le Pen presidency could also give governments further from the frontline political cover to scale back their support. For Italy, Spain, Greece, Austria, Hungary and Slovakia, Ukraine is a lower priority and Italian support could weaken further after next year’s election.
The resulting bilateralisation of aid could leave a smaller group of northern and western European countries shouldering the burden. They would struggle to compensate for the loss of contributions from much of southern and central Europe .
Le Pen would also threaten Ukraine’s EU membership prospects and the bloc’s sanctions regime against Russia. Ukraine’s membership of the EU would become virtually impossible: key decisions require unanimity, and Le Pen has already opposed Kyiv’s accession . Nor would she be alone in her reluctance. Despite their public commitments, many EU governments harbour serious reservations about admitting Ukraine.
Sanctions would be equally vulnerable. Le Pen has advocated lifting EU sanctions on Russia since 2017. The bloc’s economic sanctions are due for renewal in July 2027, and a French veto could bring them to an end. She could also block the renewal of sanctions against individuals and veto any new packages.
In short, a Le Pen presidency could simultaneously undermine the three pillars of Europe’s support for Ukraine: on financing, EU membership and sanctions on Russia .
Let us imagine for a moment the worst-case scenario – as a result of Europe’s inability to sustain Ukraine after a Le Pen victory, Kyiv is pushed into a settlement on Moscow’s terms . Russia gets constitutional recognition of its annexation of Donetsk and Luhansk (and possibly even Zaporizhzhia and Kherson). Moscow also imposes political and security conditions on Kyiv: a prohibition on Nato membership, a cap on the size of its armed forces, and the political demands Moscow dresses up as “denazification”.
After an unprovoked invasion and almost five years of ruthless Russian attacks on civilians, Ukrainians would see the deal as a humiliating defeat. The humiliation would be greater still if Kyiv signed under pressure from Washington, with support from some parts of Europe and opposition from others.
Above all, the deal would be a humanitarian tragedy. Ceding the rest of the Donbas would leave tens of thousands of civilians under Russian occupation. They would face what occupation has meant elsewhere: mass detentions, forced disappearances and torture. Others, who manage to get evacuated, would add to Ukraine’s internally displaced population.
Because any transfer of territory requires a referendum, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, would have to hold one and would probably put the whole deal on the ballot. Ukrainians would very likely reject it, opening an unprecedented political crisis. If Ukraine could no longer keep fighting, Zelenskyy would face two bad options: overrule the vote and impose a deeply unpopular deal; or resign and leave a vacuum for the next government to fill.
after newsletter promotion
Either way, protesters would probably fill the streets, opponents would challenge the agreement in court and whoever signed it would lose office. The deal would also need to clear parliament, where it could be voted down because few MPs would want their names on it. If it were instead imposed outside the constitution, politics would splinter into factions, some vowing to scrap the settlement and others insisting on moving on.
The economy is likely to follow. Donors and investors who had planned to fund reconstruction would pull back, leaving billions in potential deals on the table. The threat of Russia’s re-invasion and political instability would stall reconstruction. Millions more Ukrainians would then head west to rejoin their families, escaping a deal that fails to provide proper security guarantees and leaving economic devastation behind. At the same time, many soldiers would refuse to lay down their arms and keep up a guerrilla war in the ceded parts of Donbas. These units would be hard to rein in, possibly handing Moscow a pretext to resume full-scale fighting.
Over time, the sense of betrayal is bound to harden into resentment of western partners and Kyiv’s wartime elites alike. Most dangerous of all, Russia would probably use the pause to rebuild its economy and army. Soon, Vladimir Putin may feel tempted to exploit Ukraine’s chaos and invade again. The weak security framework of a deal on Russia’s terms would make this possible. Europe would be left with a broken, embittered and heavily armed state on its border, and an emboldened Russia behind it.
None of this is inevitable. Ukrainians have shown little appetite for capitulation, and weeks of US pressure have not shifted public opinion. Kyiv also understands that Moscow’s terms are probably designed to produce exactly this kind of turmoil. Ukraine would accept such a deal only if it had no other choice.
Getting there would necessitate a combination of things going wrong at the same time: a full US cut-off of intelligence and military support that lets Russia push the front back; European funding drying up with no bilateral substitute; and a Russian escalation backed by new mobilisation. Each is possible; together, they are unlikely. Nonetheless, this scenario should give EU capitals serious pause for thought. Policy should be built on the worst-case scenario rather than wishful thinking that Le Pen, in power, will moderate her view of Ukraine, in the way that Meloni has .
Ukraine’s outlook is bleaker than at any point since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Putin’s strategy has always been to outlast the west and achieve politically what he cannot secure on the battlefield. That prospect is becoming more plausible – not because Ukraine is losing the will to fight, or even because of Washington’s retreat, but because of what may happen in Europe next year, making it the weakest link in its own strategy to defeat Russia.
Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director for Europe at Eurasia Grou

articles.title_orig: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.title_zh: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.content_orig:
Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine
Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.
A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.
The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea , Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.
Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.
In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”
Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.
In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.
Overnight Ukraine launched 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin.
The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.
after newsletter promotion
Ukraine says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Russia’s own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. In recent weeks Russia has repeatedly hit two critical bridges in Kyiv over the Dnipro river.
Diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a “continuation of war”.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , said on Friday the Trump administration had proposed that Kyiv gives Russia the eastern Donbas region – including towns and villages Russia does not control – in exchange for Nato membership or Nato-like guarantees.
Zelenskyy ruled out handing over territory. The details of possible US security guarantees were vague and did not feature American troops on the ground, he said, citing conversations with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the real-estate developer Steve Witkoff. The emissaries last week saw Putin in Moscow.

articles.title_orig: Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda
articles.title_zh: Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda
articles.content_orig:
Five European countries announced a plan on Monday that would send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda , an experiment that comes as governments across the continent toughen their stances on migration.
The joint push from Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece was pitched as a way to handle migrants who had no right to stay in Europe but who, for one reason or another, could not or would not return to their home countries.
The project, which is not yet finalized, shows how European leaders’ stance on migration has hardened since the arrivals of 2015-16, when countries like Germany admitted more than a million asylum seekers. With far-right groups like the Alternative for Germany rising in popularity, centrist leaders have gradually taken a less welcoming stance.
“For me, today marks a crucial step toward a new migration system,” Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark, said at a news conference on Monday.
The pilot project is expected to start on a small scale, with perhaps 100 or 200 deportees. Critics are already worried both about the idea of sending people to a nation to which they have no connection, and about the risk that human rights will not be sufficiently protected in Rwanda.
The country has a history of courting migration-related deals.
Britain developed a plan to send asylum seekers there in 2022, though judges in London ultimately ruled the effort unlawful and it was later abandoned. The United States has recently deported people to Rwanda.

articles.title_orig: New Data Paves the Way for Weight-Loss Drugs for Young Children, but Questions Remain
articles.title_zh: New Data Paves the Way for Weight-Loss Drugs for Young Children, but Questions Remain
articles.content_orig:
New results from a closely watched clinical trial showed that weight-loss drugs are effective for children as young as 6, though some doctors say they are concerned about the prospect of prescribing these medications to such young patients.
The study, presented Monday at the medical conference Obesity Week, examined children ages 6 to 11 who were taking semaglutide, the compound in Ozempic and Wegovy. Most children in the trial had severe obesity, meaning they had a body mass index of 35 or higher. After 68 weeks, nearly 40 percent of those who took the drug no longer had obesity, compared with none of the patients on a placebo.
Novo Nordisk, the drug’s maker, said it would ask the Food and Drug Administration to approve the medication for this age group. The drug is already authorized for children 12 and over. Another new study, also presented at the conference, showed that the weight-loss drug tirzepatide was effective in children age 12 and older.
Doctors widely agree that more needs to be done to address obesity, which affects roughly one in five children and adolescents nationwide. But they are divided over whether powerful GLP-1 drugs, which rewire the brain’s relationship to food, are the right approach. Some are concerned about the potential long-term implications of putting children who are still growing on a drug that erases appetite and can lead people to consume very few calories.
In October, the World Health Organization cautioned against using weight-loss drugs in children under 10, citing a lack of evidence on their effects on children’s growth, development and mental health.
“The question is: Is this the right thing to do?” said Dr. Robert Lustig, a professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco. “Not, does it work? Of course it works. But is it the right thing?”

articles.title_orig: Russell Brand prison message 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says
articles.title_zh: Russell Brand prison message 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says
articles.content_orig:
A message by Russell Brand to his followers in which he claimed innocence for his sexual offences was "clearly appalling" and is being urgently investigated, Downing Street has said.
The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
His wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, in which the convicted rapist claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."
No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.
Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the broadcast of a statement from Russell Brand is "completely unacceptable".
In a post on X, Norris wrote: "Prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims.
"This is being urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules."
In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can be seen sitting on a sofa and is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.
Relaying the message from her husband, Laura Brand said the comedian - who is currently being held at HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire - called prison staff "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".
She said she had been speaking to him and he "is OK and is praying".
Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.
Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.
"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."
Speaking earlier, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Sky News: "His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it's revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments."
"No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments," he added.
Victims' commissioner for London Andrea Simon said the claims will "certainly retraumatise his victims and other survivors of rape who have to hear it".
Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, she added: "The victims during the sentencing hearing highlighted how his denials and ongoing media fame over two decades had added to their pain and trauma.
"The fact survivors are still having to hear this now is really problematic and very concerning that we can't do more to protect them from it."
While freedom of expression allows convicted sex offenders such as Brand to profess their innocence, Simon said terms of service of media platforms should regulate "the way in which they get their message out".
She added that prison rules should also be reviewed to "bar those convicted of sending messages to be broadcast" unless permission is granted by the prison governor.
If Brand is found to have broken prison rules, possible punishments enforceable by prison governors can result in restrictions on social visits or loss of privileges such as access to additional time in the gym or loss of TV.
Governors can also impose proportionate restrictions on communications where justified.
This could include blocking specific phone numbers, increased monitoring of calls or restricting contact with individuals where necessary to protect victims or maintain prison security.
It come as Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy met with senior leaders in media, entertainment, arts and sports organisations as part of her call to end the culture of abuse in industries where there can be large power imbalances.
In the meeting, she asked the leaders what they were doing to create a culture where bullying, harassment and abuse are challenged, how they are empowering whistleblowers to speak out and how their safeguarding systems apply to freelance employees.
The attendees are due to report back to Nandy on the questions she asked them within the coming weeks, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said.
Over the weekend, Brand was moved from the category B HMP Wandsworth in south London to the category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, a prison that mostly houses sex offenders and has tailored programmes for them.
Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty, told LBC he agreed it was not "a good look" that he'd been moved to a lower security prison.
"I think people want to see him facing the appropriate punishment for what are appalling crimes against women and others and I think the whole episode is shocking," he said.
Meanwhile, there have been calls for a change in the law following Brand's conviction so that sexual relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal. The government says a discussion is to take place.
Mia Latter, who has alleged she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16, is among those campaigning for ministers to introduce a staggered age of consent.
She was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. Brand denied the allegations at the time. None of the women were complainants in his recent criminal trial.
Latter, who was known under the pseudonym "Alice" in the 2023 investigation, has now waived her right to anonymity.
In an interview with LBC on Monday, Latter said: "We don't want to criminalise anybody under the age of 18 [including] 16, 17-year-olds, 18-year-olds having sex with each other...
"I think healthy relationships are important, and they're important in helping you develop and grow."
But she said there should be an age "threshold" for the partners of 16 and 17 year-olds.
Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, is urging a change in the law to prevent 16 year-olds from having a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and someone aged 17 from having a relationship with anyone older than 20.
She told BBC Breakfast that "predators know exactly what they are doing".
Asked about the issue on BBC Breakfast, the foreign secretary said: "I think the reason why it's right to have this debate is we've seen some of the very, very brave victims of Russell Brand come forward and say 'we think this needs looking at'".
Shadow education secretary Laura Trott said she is glad there is a conversation around staggering the age of consent but warned that it had "been quite complicated to actually implement" in some US states where it is used.
Trott said a suggestion that the age of consent should be raised to 18 is also a "conversation we need to have" but "probably isn't practical".
Anna Edmundson, director of policy & social change at the NSPCC charity, said: "We urgently need a review of what is and isn't working to ensure 16 and 17-year-olds are fully protected in law from this predatory behaviour.
"However, closing these gaps will only be part of the solution. We must question why adults have been able to exploit teenagers in plain sight for so long, and look at what further action is needed to help people recognise the signs of exploitation."
Any change in the law would only affect England and Wales as Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate legislative powers in relation to the age of consent, which is also currently set at 16 in both nations.
The Scottish Government said it had "no current plans" to change the age of consent, following the calls by campaigners, but any proposals would be considered.
The foreign secretary also apologised for having appeared on Russell Brand's online show in 2015, when he was Labour leader.
Miliband told Today if he'd known about the allegations then, he would not have done spoken to him, adding: "I deeply regret doing that interview and all my sympathies are with those victims."

articles.title_orig: Trump says he might meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China
articles.title_zh: Trump says he might meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China
articles.content_orig:
Trump's trip comes amid the Nvidia CEO scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As he departed the White House Monday morning, Trump said he "may" meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China as well, though he said it would ultimately be Xi's decision.
"He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump said of Kim Jong Un.
Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials said they do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will have a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral, though Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
The president's trip comes as questions linger about what the administration knew about prominent tech CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels. Officials did not specify his reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to Musk's business interests in China.
An official said they expect some additional U.S. business leaders to be attending the APEC CEO Summit, but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump is expected to leave Washington in the morning of Monday, Nov. 16 and arrive in Manila in the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17, and will head to a bilateral meeting with the other members of the Quad, a diplomatic partnership the U.S. has with Australia, India, and Japan, about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand.
He will then participate in an ASEAN cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
The next day, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony at Malacañang Presidential Palace, the official residence of Filipino President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Romualdez Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. He will also participate in an Association of Southeast Asian Nations cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
After Wednesday’s events in the Philippines, Trump travels to Shenzhen, China, where it is expected that a minister will greet Trump on the tarmac. He will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon local time, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi.
The historic trilateral Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia swing.
Each of Trump and Xi’s meetings this year have been clouded by other topics.
When Trump visited China in May, the raging war in Iran overshadowed the state visit that was scheduled after a detente in Trump's tit-for-tat trade war. Also, when Trump welcomed Xi in September, the pomp and circumstance Trump had planned went without live TV coverage after his banning outlets from the press pool led to a network boycott.
Now, in the background of this trip, is the scandal involving Nvidia's CEO, Huang, who joined Trump's last trip to China earlier this year after boarding Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, according to pool reports at the time. Huang was reported to have had an affair with Alice Huang , a Chinese national and tech executive who is accused of being a Chinese spy.
Officials said they do not expect Trump to raise the allegations against Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, with President Xi, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Huang resigned from Nvidia's board and as its president and CEO on Nov. 12.
This scandal engulfing Huang has introduced scrutiny over Trump’s ties to him and what Trump and other administration officials knew about the relationship with the alleged spy.
"Well, I've been hearing about it and I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9.
When pressed on if he was aware of the allegations during his May trip to China, Trump said: "No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had."
On May 12, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the plot. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said.
A U.S. official and a source familiar with the matter told ABC News that after Air Force One landed in China, White House officials asked for business leaders -- including Huang -- to be allowed into a meeting with President Xi. Initially, the Chinese were hesitant to adjust the program, but ultimately agreed to it.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, one of the world’s most-valuable companies and the maker of chips that top AI companies heavily rely on, has been a constant presence around Trump, who has invited tech executives to multiple events, both at the White House and on overseas trips. Since April 28, when Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a state dinner for King Charles III and Queen Camila, the tech CEO has participated in at least six events with Trump, including the September state dinner for Xi.
Huang has lobbied for policy positions that benefit China and Chinese companies over the past few months.
For example, the U.S. has long blocked China's access to American AI chips. However, in December 2025, after lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened those restrictions -- approving the sale of some older but still powerful chips to China as part of a remarkable deal that gave the U.S. government a 25% cut of the sales.
And in July of this year, Huang joined the social media platform X to push back against possible bans on open-weight AI models, the type that Chinese companies have embraced, and which would be cheaper for businesses and governments to adopt. The ban would benefit American companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which use closed models. The U.S. was reportedly considering those bans.
"The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models," Huang wrote in his first-ever X post.
This trip marks Trump's first one overseas since American voters handed him and Republicans a devastating defeat in the midterm elections. Voter Polls show voters rejected the president’s tariffs and the war in Iran -- two of Trump's key foreign policy positions.
